title: Camp 4 close: the reed and the emperor
hookLine: seventy-five days with two books; next, the depths

lines: KONYA, AND A CAMP ON THE FRONTIER.
cards: Seventy-five days ago, you picked up two books at once. One by a poet in Konya who wrote in Persian and, tradition says, dictated his book to a student.

One by a Roman emperor, written to himself in Greek, some of it, the book's own headings say, in army camps on the northern frontier. Two men who never met, a thousand years apart, who would have found each other strange.
Both carried, both kept apart. Today the camp closes and names what it found.

teach.b: Here are the camp's words, in the order they came. Masnavi, Rumi's long poem of stories, in six books. Sufi, the Islamic mystical path he walked, and the promise to keep him whole, Quran, Prophet and all.
Ney, the reed flute crying for the reedbed. Tawakkul, trust in God, with the camel still tied.
Daimon, Marcus's divine spark within, to be honored and kept upright. Ghazal, the love poem signed with Shams' name. Sema, the turning, listening with the whole body.
And Şeb-i Arus, the wedding night, a death kept as a meeting. Around those words, the two men gave two great moods.

teach.h: FROM RUMI, LONGING; FROM MARCUS, DUTY.
teach.b: From Rumi, longing. The reed sings that whoever is parted from their source longs to go back, and that ache isn't a malfunction; it's a direction. From Marcus, duty.
Do the next thing in front of you, justly and kindly, without hurry, as if it were the last. Longing pulls you toward what you love. Duty keeps your feet on the ground where you are.
They don't merge, and they're not one teaching. But a person can carry both, the way you can carry a compass and a lantern. And now, the depths.
Camp five is the last camp of this year.
For seven weeks it visits the other doors on this app, Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Catholicism, Islam and Sikhism, one first idea at a time, told the way each tradition tells itself.
Then the Stoics, properly. Then what science can honestly say. It starts tomorrow with how to be a guest.

how: Readers who have finished a long reading of Rumi and Marcus often keep both books near: Rumi for longing and devotion, Marcus for daily duty, read a few lines at a time.

o: the divine spark within you, to keep upright
an evil spirit that leads a person astray
a Greek god who watches over soldiers in war

games.q: camp four's words — tap the pairs.
p: the reed flute, crying for home

s: camp four blended Rumi and Marcus into one teaching
they were read side by side and kept apart: longing and duty.
for Rumi, longing is a direction, not a malfunction
the reed sings that whoever is parted from the source longs to return.
camp five visits seven other doors
Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, Catholicism, Islam and Sikhism, then the Stoics and science.

games.q: you've finished seventy-five days with two books. which one do you keep?
o: both, side by side: longing and duty.
games.why: the camp's point was never to pick a winner: Rumi gives longing, Marcus gives duty, and a person can carry both without merging them.

practice: First, longing: let yourself feel what you most deeply want, the reed's ache, without fixing it, and let it be a direction. Then duty: name the one next thing in front of you today, small and plain, and let it be solid ground.
Hold both, one in each hand, and breathe between them.

wordCard.voice: Daimon. Marcus's divine spark within, to be honored and kept upright, one of this camp's own words. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: longing and duty. A compass and a lantern, carried together. Camp four is complete.
